newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-French strike impacts rest of Europe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French strike impacts rest of Europe.

text.p: The economic cost of the French truckers' strike mounted on Thursday as they tightened their stanglehold on the transport system of the country at the cross-roads of western Europe.

On the 11th day of the strike that has virtually paralysed France, volunteers distributed free sandwiches and coffee to thousands of drivers from Britain, Spain, Germany and other countries stranded in cold wintry conditions. A similar strike in Denmark was also taking its toll.
The strikes have already cost European food and haulage industries tens of millions of dollars a day. The timing in the pre-Christmas season crucial to commerce, could not have been worse.

And industry is starting to feel the pinch, even in far away Sweden where car maker Volvo said it expected difficulties maintaining production next week if the truckers' strikes in France and Denmark continue.

"I think we can keep production going today and on Friday. But we foresee great difficulties in the beginning of next week for our plants in Gent, Born and Torslanda," Volvo Car spokesman Ingmar Hesslefors told Reuters.

Karl Heinz Schmidt, managing director of the German Transport Association said 1,000 German trucks were stranded in France, costing haulers $650,000 a day. The indirect impact on German industry would be many times that, he said.
"Starting next week, consumers will see themselves that things like oranges, cauliflowers and Christmas trees will be more expensive," Schmidt told Reuters.
The impact on the car industry could worsen if makers such as Volkswagen AG have to cut back production for lack of parts from suppliers in France and Spain, he said.
In Britain, where the impact has been compounded by the fire in the Channel Tunnel which links it to the European mainland, supermarkets started airlifting fresh produce on Wednesday.
British drivers have been outspoken in their protests.

"British drivers are being held hostage. It contravenes all the principles of the single market and all decency. it is atrocious to keep people in these conditions for 11 days. There are at least 1,000 trucks caught in the blockade," Freight Transport Associtaion spokesman Adam Wurf said.
The Spanish Association of International Road Transport said 12,000 to 14,000 Spanish trucks were affected, as France is Spain's only land bridge to the rest of the world.

"November and December are the months in which transport companies make their money," association leader Eduardo Mendez told Reuters. The impact is five times worse than if the strike had taken place in January, he said.
The Spanish Agriculture Ministry estimated losses to the farm sector at some $16 million a day, but said more accurate figures will only become available after the event.
The strike also paralysed Portugal's road transport fleet, which ships tonnes of fruit and vegetables daily.

Carlos Cazenave of the national association of road hauliers told Reuters the daily cost of the stoppage for the 1,500 Portuguese trucks now stranded in France -- a third of the national fleet -- was $500,000.
He said about 90 percent of Portugal's total fleet was paralysed, with up to 3,000 trucks stuck in Portugal, unable to transport produce to other parts of Europe because they cannot cross France.
Portugal's biggest car plant, the Ford-Volkswagen AutoEuropa joint venture, was considering halting production outright from Friday if the strike went on, a spokeswoman said.
Belgian ports were clogged by lorries forced to detour from the Franch Channel port of Calais, with massive queues and lengthy waiting times to board U.K.-bound ferries.
Dutch hauliers organisation EVO said Dutch exporters were losing three to 4.00 million guilders ($2.34 million) a day or some 60 million guilders to date due to road blocks in France and Denmark.
The EVO has asked the government to provide financial compensation for the businesses hit hardest, as most insurance policies do not cover losses from this type of protest action.

ANITA (Italian medium and large hauliers association linked to employers association confindustria) secretary general Luigi Sestieri told Reuters his body had officially asked Italian govt to seek financial compensation from french government for losses. ($1=1.711 Guilder) ($1=1.5330 Mark)
